#4165. Review: Metaphor: ReFantazio (Switch 2) - An Extraordinary JRPG That Could Use Another Optimisation Pass

A game with the name 'Metaphor' that tackles issues such as culture diversity, democracy, and classism isn't exactly subtle in its delivery, but is just as poignant in 2026 as it was when the game first released in 2024.

Atlus has brought its critically acclaimed turn-based role-playing to Switch 2, and in doing so, reminded everyone of two things: That Atlus are absolute masters at delivering striking stories, endearing characters, and engaging combat through the lens of an incredibly unique art style, and that optimisation for handheld consoles is not their strong suit.

Metaphor: ReFantazio is simultaneously the story of a young boy yearning to reconnect with his dear friend, the prince of the kingdom of Euchronia who had been struck with a curse that left him in a comatose state, a story of prejudice and social manipulation through the kingdom itself, started by the assassination of the king at the hands of Louis Guiabarn, a common-born army officer wanting to challenge the status quo through true meritocracy, AND the story of the parallels between fantasy and reality, using real-life situations as elements of idealistic fantasy within Metaphor's world, things that could never happen for the residents of Euchronia.

The way that Metaphor deftly handles so many threads of varying sizes and scopes is nothing short of extraordinary, especially when the themes of anxiety, willpower, and hope are so striking in the real world.

The individual characters in Metaphor are largely brilliantly written, with their own struggles and demons to battle, even if they aren't party members or sometimes even less important to the overarching plot. Characters like the bat-like Eugief, Heismay, battles prejudice for his race whilst trying to mourn the loss of a family member, but displays his own prejudice against the rabbit-like Papirus for their part in his grief. The stoic Brigitta, owner of the capital's magic igniter shop, casts an icy exterior, only to show her true colours through a puppy she can't resist but take in.

Even the game's main antagonist, Louis, is incredibly compelling, bringing an immediate presence to the screen through his striking design and charismatic dialogue, but as is par for the course, there is far more than meets the eye with Louis. There are a lot of plates to spin in Metaphor, but almost all of them are tantalising events to keep returning to.

It's difficult not to make comparisons between Studio Zero's Metaphor and the Persona series, as they share a lot of DNA: a calendar-based system that has you not only exploring dungeons for treasure and boss fights, but also balancing improvement of social stats, or virtues as they're known here, and bonds with party members and other important NPCs to learn more of their personal stories and gain benefits to the more traditional JRPG aspects of the game in the process.

But Metaphor stands alone in Atlus' repertoire by not only drawing from Persona, but the core Shin Megami Tensei franchise as well, while infusing its own flair in its combat mechanics through the Archetype system.

Archetypes in Metaphor are much closer to the Final Fantasy series' job system than they are to Persona, with each character gaining skills and masteries through use of interchangeable classes gained through the social parts of the game, and combat-earned AP gained to level them up. MAG, a currency gained through both combat and socialisation, can be used to transfer skills from one archetype to another, giving you plenty of ways to experiment with your own builds between the seven party members and the 30 different Archetypes alone.

Combat itself utilises the Turn Icon system resembling core Shin Megami Tensei games, with extra actions gained by striking a critical hit or weakness, or serious losses by missing an attack or hitting an absorbed element. You can also strike at an advantage by attacking enemies in the overworld in real-time, or take them out entirely if you're high enough above them in level (a feature I wish all future JRPGs would carry!), but if an enemy gets the jump on you, it can be devastating. All of these elements combine to make arguably the best combat Atlus has ever put out in a JRPG.

It's also impossible to discuss the game without mentioning its frankly stellar soundtrack. Composer Shoji Meguro's unique flavour is felt throughout the game, with one of the best battle themes to ever grace a JRPG, drawing from Buddhist sutra inspirations with priest Keisuke Honryo's unforgettable chanting.

All of this is to say that Metaphor: ReFantazio is an incredible JRPG, and one that will keep you coming back over and over for well over 80 hours. However, on Switch 2, the experience hasn't come across without a few hiccups along the way.

After releasing Persona 3 Reload on Switch 2 last year, which itself suffered greatly from frame rate issues and muddy visuals, and experiencing inconsistencies with Metaphor: ReFantazio itself in its original release, I was sceptical, to say the least, and that scepticism ended up having merit, as I'm not sure I've seen a game look quite so beautiful and hideous at the same time!

From an artistic standpoint, Metaphor is sumptuous, taking the 'more is more' approach from Persona and applying a much wider colour palette; the UI and menus are stunning, of that there's no doubt. But technically speaking, Metaphor is a bit of a mess.

There are options to run in performance, balanced, or graphics modes both handheld and docked, but regardless of which mode you pick, there were inconsistencies throughout. One moment in combat could look stunning AND run well, and the next cutscene you'd encounter the strangest case of anti-aliasing and fuzzy textures, despite there only being two characters in the room.

Frame rate issues also persist regardless of performance or graphics settings, never enough to overtake the other amazing qualities of the game, but always enough to notice and occasionally distract. Persona 3 Reload did eventually get a performance update that fixed a lot of issues; suffice it to say, I truly hope Metaphor gets one as well!

Additionally, while so much of Metaphor's main dungeons and set pieces are a sight to behold, Atlus's dungeon designs have often left something to be desired, and that's apparent in Metaphor's side dungeons. When on a side quest, it's fairly easy to get turned around in the sea of brown tunnels and foggy forest areas, simply on the back of them all looking identical! It's a stark difference to the Regalith Cathedral, Sandworm's Belly, or Skyrunner main dungeons, for sure.

Metaphor: ReFantazio is an extraordinary JRPG, juggling stories and systems alike with grace and effortlessness, but it is let down somewhat by poor optimisation on Switch 2.

Anyone looking for a huge, sprawling adventure with lovable characters, compelling parallels to the real world, and progression systems that will keep you coming back for more will be far from disappointed with this game, but there's no metaphor for a dodgy frame rate and visuals that can occasionally take you out of the fantasy.

#4164. House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy

Big Walk developer House House has found itself at the center of a controversy over the upcoming Independent Games Festival on March 3, 2027, after a group of its jurors said they would not vote for any game that has used generative AI in any capacity. The jurors' statement does not name House House or Big Walk, but the studio eventually updated its FAQ to explain how it used generative AI for coding after IGF discussions. After vaguely posting on social media, those associated with IGF made clear that a sticking point in the voting process was Big Walk.

Former games journalist and game developer Austin Walker posted the IGF jurors' statement on Bluesky, explaining that voting has been difficult this year due to the "significant increase in the number of submitted games developed with generative AI tools."

"This has set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools, and at this point there is no universal consensus on what (if anything) is to be done," the statement reads. "The IGF has affirmed that we may cast our votes according to our own tastes and values. But we, as a contingent of IGF jurors, feel that this trend and the games embracing it deserve stronger pushback than a vote in silence."

The statement continues, explaining that not all jurors are on board with the blanket statement, citing reasons including "their ability to safely sign without professional blowback." It continues, "Above all: Our goal is to state solidarity with those who despair over the future of their art, their craft, and their industry – including those who have experimented with these tools, but who now believe they are not in our best interest."

The statement continues with the jurors' beliefs regarding gen-AI, including its negative effects, that any gen-AI used in any process of game development is not okay, noting specifically that "AI-generated code is not an exception to these harms," and more.

"For those reasons, this year we are declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity," the statement says. "We urge the IGF to adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work." The statement then includes the names of the IGF jurors who signed it.

Big Walk isn't specifically mentioned within that statement. However, Kyle LeClair, a four-time IGF judge and a juror for the upcoming IGF, tells Aftermath that "it got to the point where the most-discussed game this year almost entirely involved its AI usage, overshadowing pretty much everything else." LeClair says it felt like a boiling point, adding, "Anyhow, strong props to the jurors for taking this stance and putting out this letter as well, even if some people believe that using AI for coding purposes is a more gray area, we're at a point where the amount of AI slop clogging up the indie game scene means having to take hard stances such as this in order to discourage such an amount of recklessness."

Again, no mention of Big Walk. However, game developer Bruno Diaz took to BlueSky to confirm the speculation: that most-discussed game was Big Walk. "Okay, because the cat is out of the f---ing bag, I might as well combat misinformation a bit: 1. The reason IGF judges are aware of the LLM use in the development of Big Walk is through a disclosure shared by House House. 2. This disclosure was required by IGF rules. 3. While some have characterized the LLM usage as just fixing one individual blocking bug, this is a bit inaccurate; the description given by House House mentioned there being several instances, though they did also say it was mostly 'consultative' use and not code gen or agents."

Diaz notes that they believe that distinction is without a difference, adding that "to my knowledge, it is not the case that Big Walk is non-compliant with the former [Steam's AI disclosure requirements]."

"Yes, there was a large discussion about this in internal IGF forums," Diaz said. "Yes, a lot of people said things that I personally think were disingenuous, extremely disappointing, or just (frankly) dumb. No, I have no intention of talking about it in further detail or exposing anyone. [...] Ultimately, it is extremely difficult for a group of over 100 people to keep a secret so I expected this to come out eventually. Shrug emoji. If you think something is reputationally damaging, consider not doing it."

With discussion surrounding Big Walk happening during the IGF discussions, House House updated its FAQ to address, "Was AI used to make Big Walk?" Here's what the FAQ reads, in full:

"In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The primary use case for House House’s use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code. If you’re technically-minded, and curious, here’s an example. We needed to cull shadow casters by distance from the camera, but Unity URP only allows culling shadow casters by distance in camera forwards, so shadow casters behind the player were being rendered at an infinite distance. This made our game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP.

We originally wrote a version of the above disclosure as it was a suggested part of our IGF submission. We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.

This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.

Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

As you can see, House House did not disclose its use of AI-generated code because "Steam as a platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage." It says it is posting the disclosure now as "it has become a matter of public interest."

House House recently made headlines for choosing not to put Big Walk on Xbox in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft Games. Earlier this year, it gained widespread critical acclaim for its unique emphasis on cooperative puzzle-solving – you can read more about that in Game Informer's Big Walk review.

#4163. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with a decent selection of maps and modes

Battlefield 6's second-ever free trial, and the first in 2026, is upon us.

Battlefield Studios has announced that Battlefield 6 is going free to play for one week next week. Well, a portion of the game is, anyway, as part of a free trial that will include some of the game’s most popular modes and maps.

Though it does not encompass the entirety of the game, the free trial is fairly generous. Here’s what to expect.

For starters, the trial kicks off Tuesday, March 17 and will run until the following Tuesday, March 24. The trial will be accessible from Battlefield Redsec, the already free-to-play portion of the game.

Once downloaded, you’ll find a new Battlefield 6 Free Trial section in the main menu. Because Redsec and Battlefield 6 multiplayer share progression, if you played the former at any point, you’ll be able to pick up from where you left off.

The same is also true the other way around; if this is your first time with Battlefield 6, all your unlocks will carry over to the full version, as well as to Redsec if you decide stick with the free-to-play off-shoot.

Once it kicks off, you’ll find three playlists to choose from. Casual Breakthrough, All-out Warfare, and a third playlist showcasing the new Nightfall game mode and its associated map.

All-out Warfare is what you come to Battlefield for, and that playlist features Conquest, Breakthrough, as well as BF6’s newcomer Escalation - all large-scale, combined arms game modes. They will be playable across four maps. You get to play on two from Season 2: Contaminated, and Hagental Base, one from Season 1: Eastwood, and Mirak Valley from the base game.

Casual Breakthrough is based on a playlist that already exists in the core game, and it’s really designed as a nice on-ramp for new players. It also offers less intense gameplay, perfect for people grinding unlocks.

Casual Breakthrough is limited to just 16 real players (eight per team), with the rest filled up with bots. You earn the same amount of XP in those matches, except when you interact with bots, so killing a bot will net less than a human player. Outside of that, unlocks, Challenges and all other things that don’t depend on stat-tracking can be done within.

In the trial, the Casual Breakthrough playlist includes Hagental Base, Contaminated, and Eastwood.

The most interesting is the third playlist, in part because its content will also be available to owners of the full game for the first time right alongside free-to-play players. Nightfall is a playlist exclusive to the Hagental Base map.

This is a very small map, so the mode selection here is Team Deathmatch, Squad Deathmatch, and Domination. Under Nightfall conditions, lights across the entire map are turned off, so you’re going to have use your NVGs to be able to see. This is also a god opportunity to try out weapon attachments that specifically work under low-light conditions, which typically don’t get much use in multiplayer.

March 17 also marks the launch of the second stage of Battlefield 6’s Season 2, which comes with the aforementioned Nightfall content, as well as a big new update - so the timing works out nicely for everyone.

#4162. The Abxylute M6 Is An Ideal Bluetooth Mobile Controller For Those On The Go

Gaming on the go feels so much better with the abxylute M6, and you won't have to clean your screen every few minutes.

We’ve come a long way since Snake was the pinnacle of mobile gaming. Today’s phones are portable computers capable of running console-quality titles, both natively and through cloud streaming, but often these can be frustrating to play with touch controls which sorely impact the overall experience. With its M6 model, live now on Kickstarter, abxylute aims to deliver the comfort of playing with a controller alongside the convenience of portability.

On first impressions, the abxylute M6 is a sleek piece of kit, reminiscent of hardware like the Xperia Play. Your MagSafe or equivalent-enabled phone attaches via a powerful magnet, which then slides upwards to reveal the controller underneath. The magnetic island itself can be slid left or right to fit the magnetic area of your phone, and even removed and carried separately if you find it adds just a bit too much bulk in your pocket.

This marks a change from the usual telescopic mobile controllers which place the buttons to the sides of your phone, making for a very wide device, instead keeping the footprint to around the same size as a regular DualSense or Xbox controller. My M6 came with an extra attachable grip for even more comfortable holding, something I would very much come to depend on during testing.

The M6 comes with three pairing modes depending on what you are playing: PS Mode for Remote Play and PlayStation emulators, Xinput Mode for anything Xbox or PC, and NS Mode that turns the M6 into a useful extra Pro Controller for Nintendo emulation. Connecting the M6 to my phone was an easy process - I first selected the mode, held the Pair button until the LED began flashing, then selected the controller in my phone’s Bluetooth settings. My phone treated all three modes as separate controllers, but once connected for the first time, all three paired almost instantly each time I wanted to use the M6. When it was time to stop, I simply slid the top down to sever the connection after a few seconds.

Other features include vibration that isn’t too overpowering, a programmable macro button that can do pretty much anything you ask of it, and turbo mode on just about any button. With abxylute’s dedicated mobile app, you can map the controls to touchscreen games, and even import your local games and emulators for easy access. It goes without saying that it supports a wide range of games that already have native controller support.

If you like to use controllers, even while mobile gaming, you've come to the right place. Here are the best mobile games with controller support.

Overall I was impressed by the build quality of the M6. The face and shoulder buttons had a clickiness to them that I like, while the linear triggers were satisfyingly springy. The M6 uses 20° capacitive joysticks, and while they felt highly responsive, they also felt a little too loose for my liking at first. I was using a Pixel 8 Pro, and while this phone doesn’t have a magnetic component, the M6 came with an adhesive-backed magnetic ring I could attach to my phone. I also use a case with a magnetic ring built in, and the M6 had no issues holding either firmly in place.

All-in-all, I liked what the M6 had to offer in terms of ergonomics and quality, and appreciated that I could have the screen and controls centrally in my field of view at the same time.

Now, how does it perform when it’s actually being used? I firstly tested the following native Android games - Asphalt Legends, GRID Autosport, Fortnite, Final Fantasy Tactics: The War of the Lions, and Warframe - for a good spread of control schemes. These all worked flawlessly out of the box on the Xinput pairing mode, with no customisation needed, as they recognised the Xbox controller and adapted accordingly.

I used PlayStation Remote Play next, opting for a game that requires extreme precision at all times: PGA Tour. Golf games are a passion of mine, but I was a bit hesitant. I expected a double-kick of Bluetooth and streaming latency to impact my experience, but outside of the standard remote play delay, I couldn’t fault the controller one bit. I wanted to, when I shanked my first shot on the Old Course of St. Andrews straight into the drink, but in reality I was just rusty. Once I’d found my groove again, the birdies flocked back to roost. For a different kind of stress test I fired up my current game, Yakuza 3, also via PS Remote Play. This requires constant mashing of buttons and stick movement, and for the large part the controller performed really well.

Co-op gaming online has never been better than with the creation of Steam's Remote Play feature.

Generally speaking, the M6 performed almost perfectly across all the games I tested, with one slight gripe - stick sensitivity. They were a little too loose for my liking - in GRID, this meant the car swaying all over the track, making precision cornering harder than it perhaps should have been. For Fortnite, Warframe, and Yakuza, the sensitivity meant that the camera was constantly moving, and I found it hard to target enemies as a result. In the former two games the camera sensitivity can be altered in the settings, which helped, but in Yakuza this wasn’t an option. Your mileage may vary here, and players more used to stick-based action games will likely manage just fine.

What I did notice with the action games was that the holding position needed to constantly use the shoulder buttons, reaching over the triggers, meant that the controller naturally tipped backwards. Because it was already top-heavy, this meant that I needed to apply more force with my ring and little fingers to hold it in place. For short gaming sessions this wouldn’t be an issue, but for longer stints this would leave my wrists feeling fatigued, and I’d need to take breaks. The included grip is essential here, giving that added leverage to hold the controller in place without tipping, and it was more manageable when I could rest my arms against a table or my lap. I’d like to see a version of the grip that has slightly larger ‘handles’, so that your hold acts more as a counterweight without the strain.

The final game I tested was League of Legends: Wild Rift. I’m a long-time player of the PC game, but always hesitant with Wild Rift because I disliked the touch controls. The abxylute app guided me through a tutorial on mapping, and once I’d figured out the control scheme I wanted to use, it was actually a game-changing experience. I could move about as fluidly as if I was using a mouse, and abilities activated instantly. I was a much more effective player, securing kills and controlling the map compared to when I used touch controls, and it made for the best time I had with the M6 overall. I can see myself committing to playing more Wild Rift now I know I have this tool available.

As part of testing, I also gave the M6 to my nephew Toby, as he’s a serial mobile gamer and far closer to the target demographic than I am. He tested Roblox natively and Forza Horizon 6 through Xbox Remote Play on his Samsung phone, and while he had similar gripes with the ergonomics, the M6 ultimately got his seal of approval. He liked the feel of the buttons and the build quality, and was surprised by the apparent lack of noticeable latency. He felt it was a controller best suited for shorter stints, something I think encapsulates the mobile gamer of today perfectly.

The abxylute M6 is an excellent piece of kit for what it aims to do, and while it has some minor drawbacks, these don’t get in the way of actually playing games. It’s something you can keep in a jacket pocket or a small bag when you’re on the move, and enjoy a short session largely without hassle or having to deal with touch controls and grubby screens afterwards. I’d have no qualms getting Toby one of these for Christmas, and it’s seriously making me consider mobile gaming as a viable option for the many bus trips I take rather than the numerous dedicated handhelds I already own.

#4161. Pikmin 4 Is Still Great, But Dandori Academy Is Underwhelming

Pikmin 4 was released for the original Switch in 2023, and it ranks among my favorite games on the platform; I happily award it the honor of being the best Pikmin game. It looks and plays great, and Oatchi the dog makes the sometimes annoying process of managing a collection of little plant creatures willing to do your bidding much smoother.

The over-titled Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy releases November 12, and much like other comparable Nintendo games that have been ported and improved for Switch 2 (like Kirby and Mario Party), the base game is as good as it was initially and looks even better. If you skipped Pikmin 4 on Switch for whatever reason (probably because it was day one of the Barbenheimer epidemic), I encourage you to play it now. You have about a week to beat it before… something else comes out. Who’s to say.

The “big” addition here for the Switch 2 version of the game, alongside improved performance and visuals and the ability to give Oatchi verbal commands, is Dandori Academy. The Academy is an expanded time trial mode that awards medals for practicing specific levels, which you can then play and upload your high scores on specific days. For example, I can play the Advanced B level, Rockaway Cellars, as much as I want, but it only really counts if I play it on November 12. And you only get one try (though you can unlock retry tickets).

In theory, I like the unique approach to high-score battling, and the limited timeframe adds fun intensity, but this isn't what I am looking for from Pikmin. I recognize and acknowledge the design decision to place timers on your interactions in Pikmin, but it’s never been my favorite part. I like building my adorable little army and exploring, discovering, and retrieving as many unexpected items as possible. But I mostly get annoyed at the ticking clock, especially when I am watching my crew meander toward my spaceship holding a Game Boy Advance SP (or whatever they manage to find on the never-acknowledged, but potentially post-apocalyptic Earth you are exploring).

I also like having a list of missions to complete, and in Dandori Academy, there isn’t much acknowledgment of your success in practice. You can earn a platinum medal while practicing Rockaway Cellar, but it’s mainly to let you know that this is what you could earn when you play on the right day.

The main takeaway is that Pikmin 4 is still excellent, and I was grateful to transfer my save file from the Switch version (and I was tempted to start a new game + save), but Dandori Academy is not a strong incentive to return if you already played the game. It is a nice bonus and an interesting concept that reimagines the familiar time trial mode featured in plenty of video games, but the original campaign is still the main attraction.

#4160. Eikichi Iwai, Bassist of Final Fantasy XIV Band THE PRIMALS, Has Passed Away

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Music makes many games what they truly are, setting the tone and doubling down on a moment's emotions, whether somber, pulse-pounding, or chilling. Without their OSTs, many games would feel like a shell of themselves, solid without the soul. Many games have used the need for music to get musicians on the map or back into the public spotlight, creating a beautiful loop.

The EU's proposed Digital Fairness Act targets loot boxes, pay-to-win mechanics, unclear in-game prices, and subscription traps.

Final Fantasy is a series absolutely defined by its music, with truly legendary composers and artists stemming from every title. Sadly, Final Fantasy 14’s Twitter announced earlier today that Eikichi Iwai, bassist for the band made for the game THE PRIMALS, has passed away. After recently performing at the most recent Japanese Fan Fest, his passing is a sudden low blow that has staggered fans across the globe.

THE PRIMALS are the standout musicians of Final Fantasy 14, far from the only incredibly talented maestros making the music happen, but definitely the flashiest. Often brought out to live events for both their own original tracks and covers of some of 14's other greatest hits, THE PRIMALS helped forge some of the greatest tracks to grace Final Fantasy 14, and Iwai-san's absence will be deeply felt in future events.

While the rest of the musicians behind FF 14 and his bandmates on THE PRIMALS will feel the most potent loss, fans across the globe are aching as well, already holding in-game mourning vigils throughout Eorzea. Sitting by fires and playing different pieces of music Iwai worked on, fans are lamenting his passing the best way they know how, by celebrating all he gave to them.

THE PRIMALS are the standout musicians of Final Fantasy 14, far from the only incredibly talented maestros making the music happen, but definitely the flashiest.

THE PRIMALS have backed some of the most pivotal moments in Final Fantasy 14’s history, bouncing from raid layers to incredibly crucial story moments to general world traversal. As a band, they’re incredibly flexible and talented, with a good part of that grit coming from Iwai’s incredible bass play. The future of the band is currently uncertain, especially with how sudden Iwai’s loss truly was.

Eikichi Iwai passed at age 57, a titan of his craft and an incredible musician across his pursuits, charming millions who played Final Fantasy 14 and all who followed his long history with the band Chirinuruwowaka, of which he was a founding member. Never one to slow down or stop making music, with his recent showing at the latest Japanese FF14 Fan Fest being cited as one of THE PRIMALS best ever showings.

After suffering a loss like Iwai’s, it’s important to remember just how lucky we are to enjoy such incredibly skilled artists in their primes. Final Fantasy 14 has its issues, but music has never been one of them, carrying many crucial emotional scenes with next-level tracks again and again.

Close in the Distance, A Long Fall, and Rise, all written by Masayoshi Soken, show a mastery of tone and emotion across an incredible range, perfectly putting players in the mindset of the current moment. THE PRIMALS’ own coverage of tracks like Footfalls and Dawntrail gives each song life, fueled by THE PRIMALS’ incredible energy.

I genuinely believe you could find someone who cites almost every song in Final Fantasy 14 as one of their favorites, and that’s amazing. The incredible display of artistry throughout the title is a large reason why it has lasted as long as it has with the massive fanbase it has cultivated.

With live service games and MMOs like Final Fantasy 14, it can be all too easy and lucrative to fall into the trappings of consumerism, focusing on the product rather than the art. FF really doesn’t have that issue. FF14 has always felt like a title guided by the artists who create it, and after the loss of such a powerful artist, it’s up to the rest of us to keep on that path. Rest in peace, Eikichi Iwai.

#4159. New TMNT: Splintered Fate Update Adds Even More Reasons To Play In Co-Op

Super Evil Megacorp has been steadily pumping out new content for its TMNT Hades-like, Splintered Fate, ever since launch, and today, the team has added a bunch of new reasons to embark on your roguelike runs in co-op.

The new Shell Squad Co-Op Update goes live today, and as its name suggests, it's all about the multiplayer fun. This free patch adds 24 new co-op powers, eight new co-op tools and eight new co-op masteries, so you can bring the heat to Shredder and the Rat King with even more skills when playing with friends.

The update also includes improved flame visuals, options for character swapping when playing co-op online or locally, and improved Lucky Dice communication.

Here are a few examples of the new powers and tools added in the update:

24x new co-op powers (3 per power tree). Examples: - Passing the Torch - The first player you touch while affected by Rapid Fire also gains its effects, for as long as you have Rapid Fire active. - Shared Warmth - When a player consumes a Splinter's Revive, heal all players. - Chain Reaction - Players' Specials have a chance to trigger a Chain Lightning, dealing Utrom damage per link.

8x new co-op tools (1 per power tree). Examples: - Bubble Trouble - Spawn a bubble on you and the farthest player. The bubble deals Water damage and Freezes enemies, and grants bonus Water damage to players. - Tether Beam - Tether to the closest player. Enemies caught in the beam will take Utrom damage every second. - Shadow Pact - Grant yourself and the closest player a Dark Shell. Each enemy defeated extends it.

8x new co-op masteries (1 per character). Examples: - Donatello - When using your Tool, the closest player becomes invulnerable. - Raphael - When any player lands a critical hit, they have a chance to Multi-crit instead. - Michelangelo - When using your Special, you and the closest player gain a Torrent Strike stack. - Leonardo - When activating your Special, the closest player gains Light Shell.

That's not all the news on the Splintered Fate front, either. The dev also announced its next paid cosmetics DLC: the Trench Coat Pack. Once again, it's another pretty self-explanatory one here, with all the Turtles (and the additional DLC characters) donning the team's iconic trench coats. This one is also available today, so there's no waiting around here, either!

#4157. Marvel Cosmic Invasion's Doctor Doom-Themed DLC Gives It The Post-Game Tail It Was Missing

Marvel Cosmic Invasion was a bit of a dream game for me; I loved the X-Men arcade game in the '90s, so when Tribute Games released the excellent Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge in 2022, I immediately hoped they'd revitalize other licensed brawler franchises released by Konami in the late '80s and early '90s. While we still haven't heard any word of a new brawler starring The Simpsons, Tribute did follow up its Turtle triumph with Marvel Cosmic Invasion, another throwback side-scrolling beat 'em up, this time starring Marvel's mightiest.

I played through Marvel Cosmic Invasion multiple times and had a blast, but I moved on quickly, as I didn't feel the need to collect different palette-swaps of the many heroes on offer. Even after Cyclops and The Thing joined the roster as DLC in May, I still saw Cosmic Invasion as a game in the rearview. That changes this week, as The Siege of Castle Doom not only adds two additional playable characters (Invisible Woman and Doctor Doom), but also a mode that has the potential to bring me back for more runs for the foreseeable future.

Seeing that Annihilus is threatening the universe, Doom decides to take matters into his own hands. Unfortunately, much in the way that it seems that he may try to fix the multiversal incursions in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, Victor Von Doom's solution in Marvel Cosmic Invasion – the Cosmic Inductor – would lead to untold death and destruction. In The Siege of Castle Doom, you select your team and fight your way through various floors of the stronghold belonging to the man who is perhaps Marvel's greatest villain. Your goal is to fight through the winding, randomized hallways of Castle Doomstadt, charging Reed Richards' Stabilizer and tactically bolstering your team along the way, before Doctor Doom can enact his plan.

As for the new playable characters, Doctor Doom is less agile, but his attacks pack a whallop, while Invisible Woman's force fields and speed make her the more versatile pick. I don't know that I see either of them replacing my mains from the base game, but I had fun experimenting with them throughout this mode. Regardless of which character you choose from the expanding roster, you still must traverse Castle Doomstadt before Doom achieves his objective.

Fighting through waves of enemies across differently themed and booby-trapped rooms, you encounter all manner of foes from the base game, as well as new minion types from Doom. When you defeat enemies, they drop batteries that charge your Stabilizer, letting you even the odds and stop Doom. Conversely, each time an enemy hits your character, it charges Doom's Cosmic Inductor, inching him closer to victory and making his minions faster and stronger in the process. As you might expect, the rooms get harder the deeper you go, and while each player starts with two characters to swap between, if a character completely depletes their health, they're gone for good, making it even tougher. As such, you need to keep your eyes on each character's health and swap them out when it makes sense.

As you complete each room, you can choose which path to take to augment your characters with new special abilities. True to the roguelite structure, as you complete rooms, you can also buff your characters' stats within the run. Certain rooms offer extra batteries to help your Stabilizer charge, while others offer new and upgraded equipment. There's also one that promises random events that can easily alter the trajectory of your run for better or worse. Though I often enjoyed boosting attack stats to make enemies less like damage sponges, I had to balance that against buffing their health to keep them alive and charging the Stabilizer to have a fighting chance.

Beyond the in-run upgrades and modifiers, you can also amp up the action run-over-run through upgrades in Reed's Lab, which add to the pool of modifiers you can select from at the start of each run. The expansion also adds new palettes for existing heroes, plus new music by composer Tee Lopes. While I've only done a few runs of The Siege of Castle Doom (each taking between 45 and 90 minutes, depending on how successful you are), I feel a revitalized sense of excitement for Marvel Cosmic Invasion. Tribute claims completionists can spend upwards of 15 hours in this new mode, which has me champing at the bit to dive back into what will likely be my primary way of interacting with Marvel Cosmic Invasion going forward.

Marvel Cosmic Invasion – The Siege of Castle Doom is available today on all platforms, and it is a strong addition to an already great game. You can read our review of the base version of Marvel Cosmic Invasion here.

#4156. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.1 livestream reveals a pared-back, four-week update as HoYo plays catch-up

Honkai: Star Rail will continue the Planarcadia story arc in Version 4.1, as the Star Rail Fest presents a new twist.

A new Honkai: Star Rail Special Program has concluded, which means some fresh news about the game’s upcoming major update. Version 4.1, unveiled today as Unraveled for Daybreak, is the action RPG’s next moment, kicking off on March 25.

Unraveled for Daybreak is the next chapter in the ongoing story of Planarcadia, with the Astra Express Crew now invited to a fan fest inspired by their own past journeys. The aptly named Star Rail Fest is ostensibly hosted to allow more of the citizens of Arcadia to experience the Trailblaze.

As everyone’s eyes is fixated on the grand Star Rail Fest, the Phantasmoon Games continue to be in full swing, as does the war with the Supplicants. Star Rail Fest is, however, the big focus of this update, in case it wasn't obvious.

The event is made up of three large-scale zones, each themed around past excursions of the Astral Express. You’ll get to explore the Belobog Zone, Xianzhou Luofu Zone, and Penacony Zone. Later on, you’ll also be able to visit Pearluxe Tower, the headquarters of Pearluxe Corp.

Each area will feature its own attractions, such as the balloon figures of Supreme Guardian Cocolia and the Destruction Engine, the duel against the Lord Ravager Phantylia at Scalegorge Waterscape, and the Pearluxe Tower’s Alloy King Pom-Pom model.

The hot new arrival is bumbling noirish detective Ashveil whom we've met in Version 4.0, and who becomes a playable character with this update. Ashveil is a 5-Star Lightning-Type character, on the Path of The Hunt. You’ll be able to pull for him throughout 4.1's runtime, which is slightly reduced at four weeks instead of the usual six, in order to rebalance the schedule after the extra-long Version 3.8.

In combat, Ashveil is capable of increasing Crit Damage of all allies. He can also mark an enemy as Bait, which reduces the Defence of all enemies on the field so long as this tag holds. If Ashveil uses his Skill on the baited target, he will deal extra Damage and regain Skill Points for the team.

Ashveil can bully that baited target even further by launching Hounding Pursuit. If any of his teammates attacks the Bait, he can further deliver a follow-up attack that gradually accumulates Gluttony for as long as he’s in combat. Gluttony can later be consumed to boost follow-up attack damage.

If he lands a kill, Ashveil continues to deal damage to the next enemy he attacks. That buff is transferred if that enemy is killed. Even in map exploration, Ashveil can be deadly, capable of inflicting Stunned upon enemies within a specific range.

Returning characters this patch will be Hyacine in the first half, and Boothill in the second half. Once again, due to the reduced runtime, their banner reruns will be slightly shorter than normal, at just two weeks each instead of three — so be sure to take that into account if you're planning on pulling for either of them.

Version 4.1 also adds the Wispae War Saga, a new activity where you can practice your leadership skills by commanding different types of Wispae Soldiers in the Graphia Academy. You can upgrade each one, use spell cards to alter their effects, and later face other champions. You ultimately want to play this to unlock new Wispae Companions, not to mention complete the challenges within.

Finally, Version 4.1 marks the start of a new Arcadian Chronicles phase in the Divergent Universe. You’ll be able to use Waypoint Pass cards to explore the different areas. HoYo is also bringing back Planar Fissure and Garden of Plenty with double rewards. And as ever, if you log in for at least seven days after downloading the new patch, you’ll earn 10 premium banner pulls.

#4155. Marathon’s Symbiosis Update Adds Host Of New Modes, Including Permanent PvE, Next Month

Bungie has detailed its upcoming Symbiosis update for Marathon, which introduces several significant modes next month. Chief among them is the new permanent PvE mode, which Bungie previously experimented with and promised earlier this year.

Symbiosis is headlined by Expedition, a co-op PvE destination with roguelite elements. Expedition pits teams of players against escalating challenges and offers randomized upgrades called Flash Boosts to increase their odds of success.

The Perimeter zone has also been expanded with the new Burrows and Reservoir areas. Another addition is Limbo, a new social hub for players to gather that features a firing range. You can also try out the new sword-wielding Bishop Runner Shell alongside new weapons and gear, such as the Maverick pistol, throwing knife, hack grenade, and V17 flamethrower. Lastly, you can test your skills against other players in the beta PvP Deathmatch mode.

Symbiosis arrives in Marathon on December 8. An open play week will kick off the same day, allowing new players to experience all of Marathon’s content for free until December 15.

The Symbiosis update marks Marathon's evolution into a more co-op-friendly, PvE experience as its initial focus on PvP extraction has struggled to sustain a substantial audience since its March 5 launch. Bungie announced in September that it plans to spend the rest of 2026 improving Marathon's core mechanics and features while giving players more agency for how they engage with it beyond competitive PvP.

#4153. GTA 6 Lead Says The Series Still Has “So Much To Do” In America

Rockstar Games co-studio head Rob Nelson says future Grand Theft Auto games could take place outside of America, but that the setting still has “so much to do”.

When Grand Theft Auto 6 launches in just over a week, it’s poised to be one of the most detailed and expansive open-world games of all time. Just like how GTA 5 built on San Andreas with its much bigger take on Los Santos, GTA 6 is transforming Vice City into Leonida, a whole state that’s now one big tribute to Florida instead of just Miami.

Even though Rockstar is primarily based in Scotland and the first two games in the series were set in an alternate version of London, every single GTA since has been set somewhere in America. Fans have wondered for some time whether Rockstar would ever consider going somewhere new, and we finally have an, admittedly vague, answer.

Earlier today, The Guardian published an interview with Rockstar North co-studio head and GTA 6 lead Rob Nelson about the game’s impending release. A big focus of the interview is how much work goes into creating Rockstar’s worlds and making them as believable as possible, with Nelson notably reminiscing about staying out in a Miami nightclub until 4am.

62 items, and you don't need to visit the stores in-person to get them.

After pointing out that Rockstar and GTA are famous for depicting American cities and the US, The Guardian asked Nelson about the possibility of the series having a game set outside of America. In response, Nelson said, “Never say never”, finally giving long-standing GTA Tokyo believers a little bit of hope in the process.

Funnily enough, former Rockstar developer Obbe Vermeij recently suggested that the studio was “definitely” considering letting a Japanese studio develop a GTA game.

That being said, you probably shouldn’t count on Grand Theft Auto returning to London any time soon, as Nelson noted that the team still has “so much to do in America”, even with the series being pushed to its limits with Leonida. Nelson thinks that everyone is an outsider to GTA’s version of America, which is something the team doesn’t seem in a rush to step away from.

Still, it’s about as close as we’ve ever gotten to hearing Rockstar say that Grand Theft Auto could exist outside of the US. I think everyone is expecting the eventual next game to give us a grand return to Liberty City, but here’s hoping that whatever follows that isn’t afraid to leave the States behind.

#4151. 10 Most Creative Traversal Abilities in Metroidvanias

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Movement abilities in Metroidvanias are a fundamental part of their appeal, determining both the pace of exploration and our ability to interact with the surrounding world.

The genre is built on understanding spaces, their composition, and how to traverse them, making movement a crucial variable regardless of the game's perspective, mechanics, or philosophy.

As a result, the possibilities a game enables for movement along the Cartesian plane largely determine how satisfying, tense, or rewarding a campaign will be, depending on its intended purpose.

Therefore, in order to pay homage to those video games that make the best possible use of the philosophy of moving from one place to another, here are the ten most creative traversal abilities in Metroidvanias.

One of the main problems games in this genre face when creating spectacular movement abilities lies in their limitations, as they have to be balanced so that they aren't too powerful.

For this reason, Silk Soar from Hollow Knight: Silksong is a masterpiece of design. Among all the powers in Metroidvanias that let you fly upwards, it's part of the few that properly contextualize the limits of its capabilities.

Not only do you acquire it in the game's last third, unexpectedly opening paths out of nowhere, but its use is also tied to your needle, requiring the presence of a ceiling to be used, so you can't just break the map's traversal in its entirety.

In terms of creativity, it's on the spectrum's simpler side, yet it solves a major verticality imbalance by granting you a great deal of ease in exploration without making you overpowered, which is a tremendous feat.

Going in the opposite direction from the previous entry, Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo is a constant display of reinterpreting Metroidvanias' most common forms of movement, with Walk the Dog being the crown jewel.

The game plays with yo-yo tricks to establish its mechanics, adapting them with thematic coherence to make you feel that, more than just having powers within a video game, you're learning new maneuvers to show off.

In this particular instance, it's as simple as being able to move orthogonally across the map at a greater speed, but this is maximized thanks to the bounce pads distributed throughout all areas that change your direction and make the ability the key to numerous puzzles.

Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo is brimming with ideas magnificently adapted to its setting, making it by far one of the most inventive Metroidvanias to come out this decade.

Well Dweller breaks one of the genre's cardinal rules by not including a double jump at any point in its story, though it compensates with a Slingshot mechanic that is simply mesmerizing.

The title allows you to throw your weapon and embed it in any surface to use it as a springboard and jump higher than usual, encouraging inquisitive and creative exploration in a truly compelling way.

Most of the game's movement is based on the biomes you find yourself in, whether in the form of bubbles, air currents, or elevators, and it works precisely because this direct yet versatile ability adapts to any situation.

Of course, it leaves you without any means of defense, but, like Kratos's Leviathan Axe, Well Dweller's matchstick flies back to you when you need it, which also leads to spectacular and almost cinematic moments when transitioning from platforming to combat.

If you're looking for games that subvert your expectations, try these eight Metroidvanias that totally reinvent themselves halfway through.

In terms of inventiveness, Animal Well is a couple of notches above the rest of the genre, with all its progression tools being as unique as they're rewarding.

Since the title is more puzzle-based than platforming-focused, most of its abilities are proportional to said distribution, but the Disc is a versatile component that you can use both to solve environmental puzzles and to traverse in seemingly impossible ways.

Throwing the frisbee and timing its trajectory to hop on and soar through the air never gets old, both because of how mechanically satisfying it is and because of all the paths mastering this skill opens up.

Animal Well is a sandbox where most of its castles are built through iteration and experimentation, but fortunately, you have the Disc on your side to make the journey faster, smoother, and more enjoyable.

Despite my reservations about Constance due to its short length and limited side content, its movement mechanics are some of the smoothest I've ever seen in the genre, with Paint Dive being the standout.

It functions as both a dash and a dematerialization of the character, allowing her to blend into the environment and pass through obstacles and hazards as a graceful mass of purple paint that seamlessly integrates with the surroundings.

In its abstract form, it's simply a directional boost, yet its execution is elevated by the environments, which force you to use the ability in increasingly diverse ways, ensuring it's more than just a regular push.

Given that platforming is Constance's forte, Paint Dive plays a prominent role throughout the entire campaign, making it a proportionally more important element of the game than many of the other abilities on this list.

From classic Resident Evil to Dark Souls, these are eight Non-Metroidvanias that heavily influenced the genre.

Returning to what I mentioned about Silk Soar and the problems of having very powerful abilities, the Crystal Arrows in Aeterna Noctis take the conversation to another level by granting you the power to teleport to wherever you aim them.

Certainly, they're used in many of the most excruciatingly difficult platforming sections the genre has ever seen, but also in one of the deepest movement systems.

Being able to chain together consecutive teleportations while fighting and traversing Aeterna's world quickly becomes a delight, especially once you get used to them and feel you've mastered their immeasurable offensive and defensive potential.

While Aeterna Noctis' structure doesn't fully capitalize on the Crystal Arrows, they remain magnificent and satisfying, surprisingly without ever breaking the game's sequence.

Castlevania: Symphony of the Night dares to take its most unusual ability and only make it necessary for a limited number of sections, yet the Mist Form remains an unforgettable memory for anyone who plays the game.

Becoming an incorporeal entity to pass through bars is the kind of power fantasy that only a character like Alucard can materialize, with the added significance of having achieved something so astonishing thirty years ago.

Although there aren't many mandatory instances where you must use it, the ability is a major surprise when you unlock it, primarily when it becomes an incredibly powerful toxic weapon that allows you to both move freely and eliminate all enemies in your path.

Years have passed, and I don't think I've ever been so impacted by unlocking a new ability, which only speaks to Castlevania: Symphony of the Night's timeless greatness.

Of all the innovations that Ori and the Blind Forest brought to the genre during the formative years when its heirs were still establishing themselves, Bash is undoubtedly the most prominent.

The ability to bounce off both enemies and projectiles to move omnidirectionally and reach new heights and locations is absurdly incredible from the very first minute to the last.

The mechanic was significantly improved in the sequel, yet its stellar and unprecedented appearance in the franchise's first title is a core memory of the genre, particularly due to its use in combat to stylize every fight sequence.

I must admit Ori and the Blind Forest isn't among my favorite Metroidvanias, though that doesn't stop me from acknowledging that, in terms of uniqueness, there's no other ability that truly compares to Bash.

If you're already tired of 2D side-scrolling games, I recommend you read about these ten best first-person Metroidvanias, ranked.

By 1994 standards, the existence of a video game of Super Metroid's caliber seems absolutely insane, as years have passed and the game remains so fresh and enjoyable that it's astonishing how ahead of its time it was.

People usually praise the Shinespark or the Morph Ball, which are masterful abilities by any measure, but I have to admit that what truly amazed me was the Grapple Beam and how wonderfully it utilizes Zebes' layout.

You spend much of the journey wondering what those strange cross-shaped blocks are for, and when you discover that they allow you to aim a beam that lets you swing freely, spin, and propel yourself at top speed, you can't help but be blown away.

Whether you played it back then or today, Super Metroid surprises you with its mastery at every turn, and there are so many ways I could have included it on this list that all I can do is stand up and applaud.

I'm going to lean towards modernity to define the top spot on this list and praise the work of MIO: Memories in Orbit, a contemporary masterpiece of the genre whose scale is truly breathtaking.

There are many reasons to say this, but unlocking the Striders, tendrils into legs and arms that can grab any surface to walk on walls, was the moment in its campaign when I realized I wasn't just playing a good Metroidvania.

Even though their use is limited by a stamina bar, thinking about the titanic effort it must have taken to craft each room of its vast map based on the eventual access to this omnipotent movement tool makes me dizzy.

Not only does it have fluid and pristine animation with perfect sound design, but it also blends seamlessly with exploration and platforming mechanics to make everything related to movement a true gift for players.

I've had many surprising moments with movement mechanics in the genre, yet the Striders in MIO: Memories in Orbit are unique while also being functional, powerful, and visually appealing, which is an elevated balance that's extremely difficult to achieve.

From the best bosses to essential lore explanations, these are eight Metroidvanias that hide their best content behind the most unexpected paths.

#4150. Surprising Literally Nobody, Grand Theft Auto VI Is The Most Pre-Ordered Game In PlayStation And Xbox Store History

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on Thursday, November 19. You can preload the game on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S starting today, as detailed by Rockstar Games, PlayStation, and Xbox. Alongside this announcement, both PlayStation and Xbox have revealed that – surprise! – GTA VI is the most preordered game in the history of their respective digital stores.

That's not shocking – GTA VI is, by many metrics, the most anticipated game in history, with its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, selling nearly 235 million copies since its launch back in 2013. There's also the fact that Rockstar Games is not releasing a physical edition of GTA VI, per se. Yes, you can go to a store to pick up a GTA VI box (and you can do so today, allowing you to preload the game), but inside that box will be a download code for a digital version of the game – you won't find GTA VI on a physical disc. So, naturally, many players are opting to purchase the game on digital storefronts like the PlayStation and Xbox game stores.

"Grand Theft Auto VI, the most preordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store, launches November 19," an Xbox blog post reads. "Considering the unprecedented demand, we encourage everyone to begin preloading as soon as possible to ensure you're prepared for launch day." PlayStation echoes this statement with a blog post of its own that reads, "Grand Theft Auto VI is now the most preordered game in the history of the PlayStation Store. Given this unprecedented demand, we've joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so they're ready to play on launch day."

There you have it: People are very excited about Grand Theft Auto VI.

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

For more, check out the song "Pusher" from the game's original score, then check out the GTA VI launch trailer. #4148. All the hype has already made Crimson Desert one of the biggest launches on Steam this year

We're merely days away from the end of the first quarter of 2026, and Crimson Desert has come in clutch to join the list of big sellers.

Crimson Desert, the open-world action RPG off-shoot from Korean MMO Black Desert Online, has officially launched, nearly six years after it was initially revealed. The game has been building up a lot of momentum over the years, which recently coalesced to turn it into one of 2026’s most anticipated titles.

All of it has been leading up to this moment, and the game appears to have landed smoothly, though not without controversy, as has seemingly become part of its MO.

It has not been 24 hours since Crimson Desert launched on PC and consoles, and it’s already become a big hit. On Steam, one of two stores where the game can be purchased (the other being the Epic Games Store), the game shot to the top of the charts.

The action RPG continued to accumulate more and more players on Steam, peaking at a very respectable 239,045 concurrent players (via SteamDB). Though its success was very much expected, we perhaps didn’t predict its peak would be that high.

Indeed, Crimson Desert has been in Steam’s top 100 global sellers list for six weeks, jumping up six spots to become the number one seller this week just before it launched. As we get closer to the weekend, the numbers could climb even higher.

This peak concurrent puts Crimson Desert in the same league as several of the other major releases of the first quarter of 2026. The top spot continues to belong to Slay the Spire 2, which peaked at a staggering 574,638 concurrent players. It happened just days after the juggernaut Resident Evil Requiem achieved its own 344,214 peak concurrent, which was the year’s highest up until Slay the Spire 2’s release. All three are well ahead of Nioh 3’s 88,045 peak concurrent, and Marathon’s nearly identical peak of 88,337.

Crimson Desert has seen something of a mixed reception by critics. James gave it three stars in our review, saying it “lacks the connective sinew to be truly functional,” which is a common criticism shared by other outlets. Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”

#4147. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

If you’re deep in Crimson Desert already, we definitely recommend giving our guides a look. We recently added new pages to help you figure out where to socket your Abyss Gear, how to find Contribution Points - and where to spend them, as well as more generally helpful information like how to expand your inventory, and how to reveal the map.

#4146. Australia Did It: End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business Review - Delivering Where It Matters

Australia Did It: End-of-the-world Railway Defense Business is a game I catch myself playing in my head long after I shut it off. Though it uses turn-based strategy as its base, it expands beyond the genre’s regular confines, blending elements from roguelikes, puzzle games, bullet-heaven titles, and the tower-defense genre. The result is an experience that demands wide-scale experimentation and rewards improvisation.

In a post-apocalyptic world where the Atlantic Ocean has dried up, you risk your life to ensure your shipment reaches its destination. Riding from station to station by train, you must build your team amid your many missions as various mutated creatures, malicious machines, and coordinated soldiers attack your convoy. Lore is doled out piecemeal and serves mostly as background dressing, but each time I learned more about the world, I became more curious.

To survive the harshness of the wasteland, you must use cindermint, an in-game resource gained for surviving turns and killing enemies, to spawn defenders, with three base classes to choose from. The revolver-wielding Gunslinger is your primary damage dealer, while the Radshot applies corrosive radiation damage, and the Nomad offers a close-range shotgun blast with knockback.

Those base-level characters offer solid variety upon which to build. And that’s where the main hook for Australia Did It comes in: experimentation through combination. In the midst of battle, you can merge two units of the same level to create new, more powerful defenders, influenced by the traits of those used in the merge. At the onset, you can merge two Nomads to create a level 2 Nomad with increased damage and knockback, but the real fun comes in combining disparate units to create completely new characters. Even now, more than 15 hours into my gameplay, I’m still concocting new combinations I want to try on my next run.

By the end of my first successful run, I had multiple level 6 characters, including a railgun-toting heavy, mages who steal health from enemies and redistribute it to nearby allies, a drone that can move beyond the walls of the station to attack enemies directly, and, my personal favorite, a dual-shotgun-wielding one-man wrecking crew. However, many of these higher-level units also possess drawbacks to consider, like the railgun scorching all adjacent tiles or the drone running out of battery if it’s outside the walls for too long. Though I started keeping notes in my head about which combinations led to my favorite results, I was grateful for a comprehensive compendium that tracked the tens of unit types I unlocked through this rewarding experimentation.

The meat of the experience places your squad on a 25-tile square board with enemies spawning from the four principal directions. Thoughtfulness and positioning are crucial, as each unit on your squad possesses different traits and movement efficiency, as do the encroaching enemies. Basic enemies often make a beeline toward the station, while others may take a weaving route or keep their distance and blast you at range. Improvising and adjusting your strategy on the fly is the most engaging part of Australia Did It, and when you perfectly adapt in the moment, or escape the scenario by the skin of your teeth, there are few better feelings I’ve experienced in a game this year.

Your goal in this phase is to simply defend the station and gather resources to strengthen your squad before evacuating and moving on to the next area. Considering each unit's strengths, weaknesses, and capabilities while strategically positioning them around the station takes some getting used to, especially during the more chaotic stages. I fist-pumped as I watched the train pull out of a station that was about to crumble, and I lamented the loss of high-level units I had to leave behind to ensure the survival of the convoy. The process is ceaselessly thrilling, even as you begin to see how the gears work under the hood. I just wish I could say the same about the intervening train sections.

Once you escape the turn-based strategy portion, your surviving squad members hop aboard the train and chart their route. Using a basic map, you choose your next stop, with factors like enemy types and modifiers shown to you ahead of time. The top-down train segments between station-defense stages are largely passive; the units you evacuated from the previous station automatically attack swarming enemies with the same traits and perks they have in the main gameplay areas. You can aim a focus cone to instruct your units, but you’re at the mercy of the units you’ve brought. You can trigger an ultimate ability to send your defenders into overdrive, but I rarely needed it.

While I love the idea of intentionally crafting a team that’s good at both the turn-based strategy and bullet-heaven transport sections, I was never fully engaged getting from point A to point B. Instead, I often caught myself checking how much longer before my train arrived at the next station; these sections can be completed in a minute or two, but that doesn’t alleviate the feeling that it’s a step down from the other gameplay. These novel portions aren’t bad by any means; they’re merely an average part of an otherwise excellent experience.

Looking back on the hours I poured into Australia Did It, the forgettable train segments will occupy only a small part of my memories, just as they do in each run. Instead, what will stick with me for months to come are the creative combination mechanics, the outstanding turn-based defense system, and the thrill of uncovering the mysteries of this bleak, yet engaging world.

#4145. All Winners At The Golden Joystick Awards 2026

Sam Woods is TheGamer’s Senior Reporter. He’s been in games journalism since 2020 and has undertaken a variety of roles in that time. These have included roles such as SEO Editor, Managing Editor at DualShockers, and Global Head of Gaming, and he's also been seen on the BBC. He was promoted to the Senior Reporter position in 2025 following a series of high-quality reports and exclusives for TheGamer.

Since 2020, Sam has written over 3,000 articles and specializes in telling the stories of the people behind the games. He’s interviewed the biggest game directors, some of the industry’s top talents, told the stories of how indie games came to be, and spoken to players about what really makes them tick. He’s also interviewed some of the world’s biggest musical artists to find out how the medium has inspired their work, and TV and Film actors about their roles in video game adaptations. He even hosted a PAX panel in 2021 and made a documentary in 2024 surrounding the creation of a Disney game.

Alongside this, Sam focuses on breaking news. He got the scoop on Perfect Dark’s cancellation, provided context on some AI drama, and revealed that Lady Dimitrescu’s actress would love to step back into the character’s giant shoes. These articles have been picked up by the biggest gaming sites, including IGN, GameSpot, and PC Gamer. He also loves to dive into the numbers behind the games.

Sam’s journey in games journalism has taken him all over the world. He’s covered Gamescom in Germany, Summer Game Fest in Los Angeles, and Tokyo Game Show in Japan, each on three occasions.

He’s been learning Japanese since 2024 with the intention of identifying and translating Japanese-language news and bringing it to English-language audiences first, something he’s done countless times.

Sam’s first review was 2020’s Battletoads reboot, and he’s since reviewed games in The Legend of Zelda, Super Mario, and Pokemon franchises.

Folks, awards season is here. Buckle in as the gaming world celebrates the year's biggest hits. First up are the Golden Joystick Awards, taking place right now. There's a huge array of games up for Ultimate Game of the Year in a race too close to call, with Resident Evil Requiem, Dispatch, Control Resonant, and 007 First Light among the favorites.

While it's unlikely we'll have a repeat of Clair Obscur's sweep last year, although GTA 6 may just have a chance, we'll have you covered every step of the way. Here are the winners as they happen at the Golden Joystick Awards.

#4144. An Elder Scrolls Classic Is Finally Getting the Remaster It Deserves After 22 Years

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

As a nostalgic gamer, I have a soft spot for forgotten games that were left behind by time, especially when they're part of a franchise as beloved as The Elder Scrolls.

While most players have spent the past two decades exploring Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim, one rather unusual entry in the series has been sitting on a much less familiar platform: the Nokia N-Gage. Thankfully, that's about to change!

The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey, a first-person RPG originally released in 2004, is getting a second chance thanks to an independent project called Shadowkey Reforged.

Developed by Dan Whelan, the project brings the forgotten spin-off to Windows, Mac, and Android with a new engine, widescreen support, controller compatibility, and plenty of visual and gameplay improvements. Even better, it's launching today, November 11.

Morrowind is rightfully regarded as one of the greatest open-world RPGs of all time, but it's aged badly and would benefit from a full remake.

For anyone unfamiliar with it, Shadowkey was the third entry in The Elder Scrolls Travels, a series of portable spin-offs released between Morrowind and Oblivion. Unlike the mainline games, however, it was exclusive to Nokia's N-Gage, a rather ambitious handheld-phone hybrid that didn't exactly have the longest life on the market.

That exclusivity made Shadowkey one of the more inaccessible chapters in the franchise's history. And while you could technically track down the original hardware and a copy of the game, that's hardly the most convenient way to revisit a 22-year-old RPG.

That's where Shadowkey Reforged comes in! Rather than simply emulating the N-Gage, Whelan built a new engine capable of running the original game's data and scripts on modern devices. Players can choose between a Classic mode that preserves the original presentation and a Modern mode featuring upgraded artwork, improved lighting, and several gameplay additions. So yes, it is literally the best of both worlds.

For anyone unfamiliar with it, Shadowkey was the third entry in The Elder Scrolls Travels, a series of portable spin-offs released between Morrowind and Oblivion.

The latter isn't just a fresh coat of paint, by the way. Modern mode introduces features inspired by newer Elder Scrolls games, including stamina-based sprinting, stealth, and ragdoll physics. You can also toggle individual features to customize the experience instead of committing to one preset. And if you happen to have The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind installed, there's another neat little bonus: Shadowkey Reforged can use its soundtrack and sound effects, preserving a connection between two games released during the same era, in case you want an extra touch!

Skyblivion team says a former volunteer is threatening legal action, even after the devs removed their code and rebuilt the affected systems.

Interestingly, Whelan has also been transparent about using AI during development. According to the developer, AI tools helped with coding, building the engine, and debugging, while the updated artwork combines AI-generated images with Photoshop and manual sprite editing.

Shadowkey Reforged is available as a free, unofficial project, with versions for Windows, Mac, and Android. However, there's one important detail players should know before getting too excited: the download doesn't include the original game's files. This means you'll need to provide your own copy of Shadowkey to play it – you can check more info about that on the port’s website.

Still, it's great to see such an obscure piece of The Elder Scrolls history getting another shot at life. Bethesda hasn't announced an official remaster, but Whelan's project might be the closest many players will get to experiencing this forgotten adventure without digging up a Nokia N-Gage.
